name: Lion
alt: A close-up photo of a large, golden-furred big cat with a thick mane, resting in tall grass.
facts: A male's roar can be heard from up to 5 miles away — loud enough to hear from a whole neighborhood over.
It can sleep up to 20 hours a day, making it one of the laziest big cats around.
A newborn cub can't even open its eyes until about a week after it's born.

name: Tiger
alt: A close-up photo of a large orange-and-black striped big cat walking through jungle grass.
facts: Its skin is striped too, just like its fur — even if you shaved one, the stripe pattern would still show.
It can leap forward more than 30 feet in a single bound, about the length of a school bus.
It marks its territory with a scent spray that some people say smells like buttered popcorn.

name: Elephant
alt: A close-up photo of a huge gray animal with large ears, tusks, and a long trunk reaching toward the ground.
facts: Its trunk has no bones at all, yet it's strong enough to lift a log and gentle enough to pick up a single berry.
It can sense other members of its herd rumbling to each other from over a mile away — through vibrations in the ground.
Babies sometimes suck on their own trunk for comfort, the same way a human baby might suck its thumb.

name: Giraffe
alt: A close-up photo of a tall, patterned animal with a very long neck, reaching up to eat leaves from a tree.
facts: It only needs about 30 minutes of sleep a day, often taken in tiny naps while standing up.
Its heart weighs around 25 pounds and pumps extra hard just to send blood all the way up that long neck.
Even with that towering neck, it has the same number of neck bones you do — just much, much bigger ones.

name: Zebra
alt: A close-up photo of a horse-like animal covered head to tail in bold black and white stripes.
facts: A newborn can already stand and run within an hour of being born — there's no time to nap when lions are nearby.
When startled, an entire herd bunches together so their stripes blur into one confusing blob.
No two have the exact same pattern, almost like each one is wearing its own custom-printed coat.

name: Panda
alt: A close-up photo of a round, black-and-white bear sitting and chewing on a bamboo stalk.
facts: It can eat up to 40 pounds of bamboo every single day — like eating your own body weight in salad.
Its black eye patches might work a bit like sunglasses, cutting glare and signaling toughness to rivals.
Even though it looks slow and cuddly, it's a surprisingly good tree climber and can even swim.

name: Koala
alt: A close-up photo of a gray, round-eared animal clinging to a tree branch.
facts: Its fingerprints look so much like human fingerprints that they could actually confuse a crime scene investigator.
Eucalyptus leaves are mildly toxic, so its liver works overtime just to keep it from getting sick.
Babies eat a special soft snack from their mom to pick up the right gut bacteria for digesting tough leaves.

name: Kangaroo
alt: A close-up photo of a tan, long-legged animal balancing upright on its strong back legs and tail.
facts: It can hop at speeds of over 35 miles per hour — about as fast as a car cruising through a neighborhood.
A newborn joey is about the size of a jellybean and crawls straight into its mother's pouch right after birth.
It physically can't walk backwards — its giant tail and legs are built only for moving forward.

name: Gorilla
alt: A close-up photo of a large, dark-furred primate sitting calmly in green forest.
facts: It's strong enough to bend steel bars, but mostly spends its day calmly munching on leaves and stems.
Each one has a unique nose print, just like a human fingerprint.
When it's relaxed and happy, it sometimes makes a deep chuckling sound that almost sounds like laughing.

name: Chimpanzee
alt: A close-up photo of a small, dark-furred primate with an expressive face, sitting among green leaves.
facts: It can recognize itself in a mirror, something very few animals are able to do.
It sometimes uses leaves as makeshift napkins or sponges to clean itself up.
It can run along the ground but is just as comfortable swinging through the treetops overhead.

name: Polar Bear
alt: A close-up photo of a huge white-furred bear standing on snow and ice.
facts: It can smell a meal from nearly 20 miles away, even through thick ice and snow.
Underneath all that fluffy white fur, its skin is actually jet black.
It's such a strong swimmer that sailors have spotted them paddling in open ocean, far from any land.

name: Brown Bear
alt: A close-up photo of a large, shaggy brown-furred animal standing near a forest stream.
facts: It can outrun a galloping horse for short bursts, even though it looks slow and lumbering.
Before its long winter nap, it eats so much that it can gain several pounds in a single day.
Its sense of smell is so sharp it puts even a bloodhound to shame.

name: Wolf
alt: A close-up photo of a gray, pointy-eared animal standing alert in a snowy forest.
facts: Its howl can travel for several miles across open land, almost like a long-distance phone call to the rest of its pack.
Each pack member has its own personality — some are natural-born leaders, others happily follow.
Its paw prints are sometimes mistaken for a large dog's, until you spot the deep claw marks.

name: Fox
alt: A close-up photo of a small orange-furred animal with a pointed face and bushy tail.
facts: It can hear a mouse squeak from about 100 feet away, and even pick up the sound of one burrowing underground.
It sometimes pounces on prey hidden under deep snow by diving in headfirst.
Its bushy tail helps it balance while running and curls around its body like a built-in blanket while it sleeps.

name: Cheetah
alt: A close-up photo of a slender, spotted cat crouched low and ready to sprint across grassland.
facts: It can go from a standstill to full speed faster than most sports cars.
Unlike other big cats, it can't fully retract its claws — they work a bit like the spikes on running shoes.
It can't roar like a lion — instead, it chirps, almost like a bird.

name: Leopard
alt: A close-up photo of a spotted golden cat resting on a tree branch.
facts: It's strong enough to drag prey twice its own weight straight up into a tree.
It can leap an incredible distance in a single bound, both forward and straight up.
Its spots are arranged in a one-of-a-kind pattern, completely unique to each individual.

name: Hippopotamus
alt: A close-up photo of a huge, round gray animal mostly submerged in muddy river water.
facts: It can hold its breath underwater for about 5 minutes, even while it's fast asleep.
Despite living mostly in water, it actually can't swim — it walks or bounces along the riverbed instead.
Its huge yawn isn't friendly at all — opening its mouth that wide is really a warning to back off.

name: Rhinoceros
alt: A close-up photo of a massive gray animal with thick skin and a large horn on its snout.
facts: Its horn keeps growing throughout its whole life, just like your fingernails.
Small birds often ride along on its back, eating bugs and chirping a warning if danger gets close.
Despite its enormous size, it can sprint faster than a human can run.

name: Crocodile
alt: A close-up photo of a long, scaly reptile floating at the surface of murky water with just its eyes and snout showing.
facts: It hasn't changed much in millions of years — its ancestors looked similar even when dinosaurs roamed the earth.
It can't chew its food, so it swallows large chunks whole or twists off bite-sized pieces.
It can stay almost perfectly motionless for hours, looking just like a floating log.

name: Flamingo
alt: A close-up photo of a tall pink bird standing on one thin leg in shallow water.
facts: Chicks are actually born gray or white — they only turn pink after eating enough of their shrimpy diet.
It can sip water that's almost boiling hot, straight from volcanic lakes.
Standing on one leg might actually help it conserve body heat while wading in chilly water.

name: Peacock
alt: A close-up photo of a bird with a spectacular fan of blue and green eye-spotted tail feathers.
facts: Its giant tail can have over 200 feathers, each one stamped with its own eye-shaped pattern.
It can run surprisingly fast along the ground when it doesn't feel like flying off.
It shakes its tail feathers to make a rattling sound that humans barely notice but other birds pick up instantly.

name: Owl
alt: A close-up photo of a round-faced bird with big forward-facing eyes, perched on a branch at night.
facts: It has extra neck bones, which is exactly why it can rotate its head about three-quarters of the way around.
Some kinds fly almost completely silently, thanks to special feathers that muffle sound.
It swallows small prey whole, then later coughs up a tidy little pellet of the leftover bones and fur.

name: Eagle
alt: A close-up photo of a large bird of prey with a sharp curved beak, soaring with wings spread wide.
facts: Its eyesight is so sharp it could spot a rabbit from almost two miles away.
It can dive toward the ground at speeds over 100 miles per hour while hunting.
Some build nests that end up weighing as much as a small car after adding to them year after year.

name: Penguin
alt: A close-up photo of a black-and-white bird standing upright on ice.
facts: It can launch straight up out of the water onto an ice ledge, almost like a torpedo with flippers.
Some dads sit on the eggs for months without eating a single bite, losing almost half their body weight.
It can swim faster underwater than most Olympic swimmers can move across the surface.

name: Dolphin
alt: A close-up photo of a sleek gray sea animal leaping out of blue ocean water.
facts: Each one might have its own unique whistle, almost like a name, that the rest of its group recognizes.
It sleeps with only half of its brain at a time, keeping one eye open to watch for danger.
It sometimes surfs the waves made by passing boats, seemingly just for fun.

name: Octopus
alt: A close-up photo of a soft-bodied sea creature with eight long arms spread across a rocky reef.
facts: It has nearly 2,000 tiny suckers, and each one can actually taste whatever it's touching.
It can squeeze its entire boneless body through a hole no bigger than a coin.
If it loses an arm, it can simply grow a brand new one.

name: Sea Turtle
alt: A close-up photo of a large turtle with a patterned shell swimming through clear blue ocean water.
facts: It might swim thousands of miles across the ocean, then return to lay eggs on the very same beach where it hatched.
Its shell is actually fused to its skeleton — it's not something it could ever take off.
Hatchlings use the glow of moonlight over the ocean to help them find their way to the water.

name: Shark
alt: A close-up photo of a large, gray fish with a pointed fin gliding through open ocean water.
facts: Some kinds have been swimming the oceans since long before dinosaurs ever existed.
Its skin is covered in tiny tooth-like scales, rough enough that it was once used like sandpaper.
It can detect the faint electric signals given off by a beating heart hidden in the sand.

name: Ostrich
alt: A close-up photo of a tall, long-necked bird with fluffy feathers standing on the open plains.
facts: Its powerful kick is strong enough to seriously injure a lion.
Its eggs are the largest of any bird — a single one could make an omelet for an entire family.
Despite the popular myth, it doesn't actually bury its head in the sand.

name: Camel
alt: A close-up photo of a tan animal with one or two humps on its back, standing in a sandy desert.
facts: It can gulp down over 30 gallons of water in just a few minutes once it finally reaches a watering hole.
Its nostrils can close completely to keep out blowing desert sand.
It has a special set of eyelids and extra-long lashes that work almost like built-in goggles.
